hints: Picture $u$ as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. For the horizontal side, think whether it is adjacent to the $50^{\circ}$ angle at the ground.
walkthrough:
**Resolve Along the Horizontal**
You can treat the launch velocity as a vector that splits into two independent parts, horizontal and vertical. The horizontal part is the side adjacent to the $50^{\circ}$ angle, so it uses cosine.

**Calculate the Value**
$$u_x = u \cos\theta = 12 \cos 50^{\circ} = 7.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
This stays constant all the way to Q because there is no horizontal acceleration when air resistance is negligible.

hints: Now look for the vertical side of the same velocity triangle. Think whether this side is opposite the $50^{\circ}$ angle and what ratio that suggests.
walkthrough:
**Resolve Along the Vertical**
The vertical part is the side opposite the $50^{\circ}$ angle, so it uses sine. This is the part that will be changed by gravity.

**Calculate the Value**
$$u_y = u \sin\theta = 12 \sin 50^{\circ} = 9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Keep this value for the next parts, it controls the time to the top and the maximum height.

hints: Focus only on vertical motion from P to Q. What must the vertical velocity be instantaneously at the highest point Q?
Link that starting vertical speed of $9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, the final speed at Q, acceleration $-g$, and height $h$ with a SUVAT equation that does not need time.
walkthrough:
**Use the Condition at the Top**
Going up, gravity slows the vertical motion at $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards. At the very top Q the ball momentarily stops moving up before it starts coming down, so vertical velocity $v_y = 0$.

**Apply SUVAT Vertically**
Take upwards as positive, so $u = +9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, $a = -9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and displacement is height $h$:
$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$
$$0 = 9.2^2 + 2(-9.81)h$$

**Show the Height**
$$h = \frac{9.2^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 4.3 \text{ m}$$
This matches the required value, confirming the calculation.
Final answer: At Q, $v_y = 0$. Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ vertically: $0 = 9.2^2 - 2 \times 9.81 \times h$, giving $h = 4.3 \text{ m}$.

hints: PQ is the straight line from launch to the top, not the curved path. You already know its vertical side is $4.3 \text{ m}$, so you need to find its horizontal side first.
Find the time to reach Q by thinking how long gravity at $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ takes to reduce the $9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ upward speed to zero.
During that same time the horizontal motion has no acceleration, so horizontal distance is simply constant horizontal speed multiplied by time.
Combine the perpendicular horizontal and vertical displacements to get the straight-line magnitude.
walkthrough:
**Find the Time to Reach Q**
Vertically, velocity falls from $9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to zero under $g$. Using $v = u + at$ upwards:
$$0 = 9.2 - 9.81t$$
$$t = \frac{9.2}{9.81} = 0.94 \text{ s}$$

**Find the Horizontal Distance to Q**
Horizontally there is no acceleration, so the $7.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ speed is constant for this whole time:
$$x = u_x t = 7.7 \times 0.938 = 7.2 \text{ m}$$
This is the base of the right-angled triangle P to Q.

**Combine to Get Straight-Line Displacement**
PQ is the hypotenuse with vertical side $h = 4.3 \text{ m}$ and horizontal side $x = 7.2 \text{ m}$. By Pythagoras:
$$PQ = \sqrt{x^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{7.23^2 + 4.3^2}$$
$$PQ = 8.4 \text{ m}$$
Final answer: Time to Q $t = 0.94 \text{ s}$, horizontal distance $x = 7.2 \text{ m}$, displacement $PQ = \sqrt{4.3^2 + 7.2^2} = 8.4 \text{ m}$.
